lesson.title: Named Tuples: Fields With Names Instead of Mystery Indexes
lesson.summary: collections.namedtuple builds a tuple subclass whose fields can be accessed by name as well as by position, keeping tuples' speed and immutability while making the code that reads them far easier to understand.
lesson.body:
You already know a plain tuple: an ordered, immutable sequence you access by position, like point = (3, 4) and then point[0] for the x-coordinate. That works, but it asks the reader to remember what index 0 means. In a tuple with five or six fields, point[3] tells you nothing on its own, you have to go find the line where the tuple was built to know which value that is. Named tuples fix exactly this readability problem.

A named tuple, built with the namedtuple function from the collections module, the same standard-library module that holds several of the specialized container types in this unit, creates a new tuple subclass with named fields. You still get every property of a regular tuple: it is ordered, immutable once created, and can be indexed by position. But you also get attribute-style access by name, which makes the code that reads it self-documenting.

```python
from collections import namedtuple

Point = namedtuple("Point", ["x", "y"])
p1 = Point(3, 4)
print(p1)
print(p1.x, p1.y)
print(p1[0], p1[1])

distance = (p1.x ** 2 + p1.y ** 2) ** 0.5
print(distance)
```

The first line after the import creates Point as a new type, not an instance, it is a factory that stitches together a tuple subclass with x and y as its named fields. p1 = Point(3, 4) then creates an actual named tuple instance. Printing p1 shows a readable repr rather than a bare (3, 4), and both p1.x and p1[0] refer to the exact same value, 3, because named tuples support both access styles simultaneously. The output is:

```
Point(x=3, y=4)
3 4
3 4
5.0
```

The distance calculation confirms it: 3 squared is 9, 4 squared is 16, their sum is 25, and the square root of 25 is 5.0. Because named tuples remain immutable, just like regular tuples, you cannot accidentally do p1.x = 10 later and corrupt a point that other parts of your program are relying on, that immutability is a feature, not a limitation, especially when you are passing data between functions and want a guarantee it will not change underneath you. Reach for a named tuple whenever you find yourself building small, fixed-shape records, coordinates, RGB colors, database rows, and catch yourself tempted to remember what record[2] means.
